articleHeadline: Five Groups of People at High Risk of Severe Complications from Seasonal Infectious Diseases
articleSummary: Five groups are at high risk of severe complications from seasonal infectious diseases such as influenza, dengue, hand-foot-mouth disease, measles, and chickenpox. Children under 5 have immature immunity and smaller airways, increasing risk of pneumonia and respiratory failure, and potential neurological or cardiovascular complications from hand-foot-mouth disease. People 65 and older experience immune aging, making influenza prone to secondary pneumonia, and dengue to severe hemorrhage or multi-organ failure. Pregnant women have altered immunity and greater risk of severe pneumonia from influenza, measles, or chickenpox; dengue can threaten mother and fetus, including miscarriage, preterm birth, or hemorrhage at delivery. Adults with chronic conditions (diabetes, asthma, COPD, heart/kidney/liver disease) see exacerbations and higher mortality. Immunocompromised individuals (cancer patients on chemo/radiation, transplant recipients, autoimmune on high-dose steroids, HIV/AIDS) face severe disease from typically mild infections. Prevention emphasizes full vaccination, protecting household contacts, limiting exposure, good nutrition and exercise, and timely medical care.

articleHeadline: Can you catch hepatitis B from sharing a meal with someone who is infected?
articleSummary: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) does not spread through eating or sharing meals. Transmission occurs mainly from mother to child at birth, via blood and body fluids (shared needles, razors, non-sterile instruments), and unsafe sex. In Vietnam, Globocan 2022 reports about 26,500 new HBV cases and 23,000 deaths annually. Babies infected at birth may be asymptomatic but HBV can silently damage the liver, increasing the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma later in life. Rarely, HBV transmission could occur if blood from an infected person contacts an open wound, but this risk is low and not a reason to isolate or eat separately. Prevention centers on vaccination: adults get 3 doses over 6 months (with pre-vaccination testing and antibody monitoring); children receive the first dose within 24 hours of birth and complete a 5- or 6-dose schedule. Additional measures include avoiding shared sharp instruments, practicing safe sex, and regular liver monitoring for infected individuals.

articleSummary: Parasites are evolving faster under human-driven pressures. Recurrent mass drug administration without sanitation improvements selects for drug-resistant parasites. In Indonesia, Papua has high malaria incidence; deforestation and population movement may drive spread. One Health approaches must incorporate evolutionary dynamics, monitor drug efficacy, vector ecology, climate, and environmental change from upstream to downstream.
